title: Punctuation Repair
intro: Commas, apostrophes and capitals: the details Cambridge examiners actually mark.

A2.q: Capitals and commas — which is correct?
options: My name is Ana, and I live in Valencia.
my name is Ana and i live in valencia
My name is Ana and, I live in Valencia.
A2.why: Names, places and the sentence start need capitals; a comma before “and” joins the two ideas.

options: It's Monday.
Its Monday.
its monday.
A2.why: “It's” = “it is”, and days of the week always start with a capital.

options: I like apples, oranges and bananas.
I like apples oranges and bananas.
I like, apples, oranges and bananas.
A2.why: Commas between the items, “and” before the last one, and no comma after the verb.

options: Where are you from?
Where are you from.
where are you from?
A2.why: A question starts with a capital and ends with a question mark.

options: She doesn't like coffee.
She doesnt like coffee.
She dose'nt like coffee.
We went to Madrid in April.
we went to madrid in april.
We went to madrid in April.
A2.why: Cities and months take capitals in English, unlike Spanish.

options: My brother's car is red.
My brothers car is red.
My brothers' car is red.
A2.why: One brother owns the car: brother + 's.

options: Yes, I do.
Yes I do
yes, I do.
A2.why: A capital at the start, a comma after “Yes”, and a full stop at the end.

A2.q: they're / their / there — which is correct?
options: They're at home.
Their at home.
There at home.
A2.why: “They're” = “they are”. “Their” shows ownership; “there” is a place.

options: My doctor is from Seville.
my doctor is from seville.
My doctor is from seville.
A2.why: Start the sentence with a capital; city names always take one too.

options: Is the sheriff in town?
Is the sheriff in town.
is the sheriff in town?
A2.why: A question starts with a capital and ends with a question mark.

options: We aren't hungry.
We arent hungry.
We are'nt hungry.
A2.why: “Aren't” = “are not”; the apostrophe goes where the “o” was.

options: If it rains, we'll stay in.
If it rains we'll stay in.
If it rains, well stay in.
B1.why: A comma after the “if” clause, and “we'll” = “we will” needs its apostrophe.

options: London, which is huge, is expensive.
London which is huge is expensive.
London, which is huge is expensive.
B1.why: Extra information about London goes between two commas.

options: “I'm tired,” she said.
“I'm tired” she said.
“Im tired,” she said.
B1.why: In direct speech the comma goes inside the quotation marks, and “I'm” needs its apostrophe.

options: It's been years since we met.
Its been years since we met.
It's been year's since we met.
B1.why: “It's been” = “it has been”; “years” is a simple plural, with no apostrophe.

options: The children's toys are everywhere.
The childrens' toys are everywhere.
The childrens toys are everywhere.
B1.why: “Children” is already plural, so just add 's.

options: However, I disagree.
However I disagree.
However; I disagree.
B1.why: “However” at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.

options: She likes cooking, reading and swimming.
She likes cooking reading and swimming.
She likes, cooking, reading and swimming.
B1.why: Commas separate the list items; no comma straight after the verb.

options: Whose bag is this?
Who's bag is this?
Whose bag is this.
B1.why: “Whose” asks who owns it, and a question needs a question mark.

options: I can't come; I'm working late.
I can't come, I'm working late.
I cant come; I'm working late.
B1.why: Two full sentences with no linking word: a semicolon, not a comma.

options: “Hands up,” shouted the sheriff.
“Hands up” shouted the sheriff.
“Hands up,” shouted the Sheriff.
B1.why: The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark; “sheriff” here is just a job, so lowercase.

options: Therefore, we stayed at home.
Therefore, we stayed, at home.
Therefore; we stayed at home.
B1.why: “Therefore” at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.

options: Semmelweis's idea was simple: wash your hands.
Semmelweis idea was simple: wash your hands.
Semmelweis's idea was simple, wash your hands.
B1.why: Name + 's shows possession, and a colon introduces what the idea was.

options: The report, which took weeks, was ignored.
The report which took weeks was ignored.
The report, which took weeks was ignored.
B2.why: Extra information gets a comma at both ends.

options: It's the company's policy; everyone must comply.
It's the company's policy, everyone must comply.
Its the company's policy; everyone must comply.
B2.why: Two closely linked full sentences: a semicolon, not a comma. “It's” = “it is”.

options: Having finished the exam, the students left.
Having finished the exam the students left.
Having finished the exam, the students', left.
B2.why: A comma closes the participle clause before the main subject.

options: He said he'd call — he never did.
He said he'd call he never did.
He said hed call — he never did.
B2.why: A dash adds a sharp, surprising follow-up; “he'd” = “he would”.

options: The 1990s were transformative.
The 1990's were transformative.
The 1990s' were transformative.
B2.why: Decades are simple plurals: no apostrophe.

options: Everyone's invited: students, parents and teachers.
Everyones invited: students, parents and teachers.
Everyone's invited, students, parents and teachers.
B2.why: A colon introduces the list that explains “everyone”.

options: Whoever arrives first gets the seats.
Whoever arrives first, gets the seats.
Whoever, arrives first, gets the seats.
B2.why: Never put a comma between a subject (Whoever arrives first) and its verb.

options: It was a well-known problem.
It was a well known problem.
It was a well-known-problem.
B2.why: Before a noun, a compound adjective like “well-known” takes a hyphen.

options: She asked whether we'd finished.
She asked whether we'd finished?
She asked wether we'd finished.
B2.why: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop.

options: The posse had one aim: to catch the outlaws.
The posse had: one aim to catch the outlaws.
The posse had one aim; to catch the outlaws.
B2.why: A colon introduces what the aim is; a semicolon needs a full sentence after it.

options: She was a forty-year-old surgeon.
She was a forty year old surgeon.
She was a forty-years-old surgeon.
B2.why: An age before a noun is hyphenated, and “year” stays singular.

options: The Lonja, which was built in the 15th century, is a World Heritage Site.
The Lonja which was built in the 15th century is a World Heritage Site.
The Lonja, which was built in the 15th century is a World Heritage Site.
B2.why: Extra information about a named building: a comma at both ends.

options: The data — startling as it was — went unpublished.
The data — startling as it was, went unpublished.
The data startling as it was — went unpublished.
C1.why: Paired dashes work like brackets: one opens the aside, one closes it.

options: He's the author whose novel won.
He's the author who's novel won.
Hes the author whose novel won.
Its impact, however, remains unclear.
It's impact, however, remains unclear.
Its impact however remains unclear.
C1.why: “Its” is possessive, and mid-sentence “however” takes commas on both sides.

C1.q: Possessives of time — which is correct?
options: A decade's worth of research was lost.
A decades worth of research was lost.
A decades' worth of research was lost.
C1.why: One decade's worth: one decade, so 's.

options: The committee agreed; the directors, however, did not.
The committee agreed, the directors, however, did not.
The committee agreed; the directors however did not,
C1.why: A semicolon joins the two clauses; “however” inside the second takes commas.

options: “Stop,” he whispered, “before it's too late.”
“Stop” he whispered “before it's too late.”
“Stop,” he whispered, “before its too late.”
C1.why: “He whispered” breaks the speech: commas on both sides, and “it's” = “it is”.

options: Twenty-first-century readers expect brevity.
Twenty first century readers expect brevity.
Twenty first-century readers expect brevity.
C1.why: A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated all the way through.

options: The team — engineers, designers and writers — shipped early.
The team — engineers, designers and writers shipped early.
The team, engineers, designers and writers — shipped early.
C1.why: Paired dashes enclose the list; leaving one out breaks the sentence.

options: Had I known, I wouldn't have asked.
Had I known I wouldn't have asked.
Had I known, I wouldn't of asked.
C1.why: A comma after “Had I known”, and always “wouldn't have”, never “wouldn't of”.

C1.q: Semicolons in a list — which is correct?
options: The posse came from Tombstone, Arizona; Dodge City, Kansas; and Abilene, Texas.
The posse came from Tombstone, Arizona, Dodge City, Kansas, and Abilene, Texas.
The posse came from Tombstone; Arizona, Dodge City; Kansas, and Abilene; Texas.
C1.why: When list items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items.

options: Hippocrates' ideas shaped medicine for centuries.
Hippocrate's ideas shaped medicine for centuries.
Hippocrates ideas shaped medicine for centuries.
C1.why: Classical names ending in -es usually take just an apostrophe: Hippocrates'.

options: Did he really say “Valencia never sleeps”?
Did he really say “Valencia never sleeps?”
Did he really say, “valencia never sleeps”?
C1.why: The whole sentence is the question, so the question mark goes outside the quotation marks.
